verdicts.exploit_preconditions: Beyond the policy itself the attacker needs, in order: (1) THE GRANT — anon or authenticated must hold INSERT on public.auth_password_set_intents. UNKNOWN from the repo: 000_baseline.sql is a --no-privileges pg_dump (zero GRANT statements), no migration grants or revokes anon on this table, and 164's app_tenant default privileges do not cover it. Resolving this requires live DB access (`\dp public.auth_password_set_intents` / `SELECT * FROM information_schema.role_table_grants WHERE table_name='auth_password_set_intents'`). Supabase's platform default and migration 107:4-8 (which states sibling auth tables "were readable with the public anon key" in this very project) both point to the grant being present, but neither is verification. (2) THE KEY — the Supabase project URL plus the anon key. Repo evidence shows this deployment does not publish them: no NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_* in any app source, no browser-side Supabase client, all DB access is server-side via the gateway's service_role. The attacker must obtain the anon key by other means (leak, misconfigured frozen developer-portal build, or CI/env exposure). (3) A TARGET user_id — obtainable from the intents table itself via the same USING(true) SELECT (it stores user_id + email for every merchant who completed OTP verification since 078); users_custom is NOT anon-readable (locked to service_role by 107:33-35) and /api/auth/lookup does not return ids. (4) Nothing else. With (1)+(2)+(3) the attacker INSERTs a row with a self-chosen id, the victim's user_id/email, and a far-future expires_at; sets cookie lb_password_set_intent=<that id>; sets letbuyy_csrf cookie and a matching X-CSRF-Token header (double-submit, attacker controls both); POSTs /api/auth/set-password once (limit 5/15min per IP). No token secret, no HMAC, no expiry the attacker doesn't control, no single-use barrier, no email-ownership proof, no device or session binding, and no "already has a password" check stand in the way. Scope is public.users_custom (merchant/platform accounts) only — NOT storefront customers.
verdicts.remediation: Add a new migration mirroring the 107 + 163 pattern exactly: `DROP POLICY IF EXISTS "Service role manages auth password set intents" ON public.auth_password_set_intents; CREATE POLICY "Service role manages auth password set intents" ON public.auth_password_set_intents FOR ALL TO service_role USING (true) WITH CHECK (true); REVOKE ALL ON TABLE public.auth_password_set_intents FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated;` — the REVOKE is required as defence in depth precisely because the grant state cannot be established from the repo. Safe for the gateway: it connects with the service_role key, which bypasses RLS (107:17-19). Then close the systemic hole that let this through the 107-validator gate: scripts/validators/foundation-sql-policy-residue-validator.mjs:46-54 must stop treating a policy NAME containing "service role"/"service_role" as proof of scoping, and instead require a literal `TO service_role` clause on any USING(true)/WITH CHECK(true) policy. Re-run the residue validator afterwards and expect it to surface any other name-only-whitelisted policies. Finally, harden the flow so a single DB row is never sufficient: make the intent cookie a signed/HMACed value binding the intent id to the verified email and the OTP device fingerprint, and have the gateway consume path verify that binding. Authority class: this is an RLS/identity change on the auth path — per CLAUDE.md it requires ARB approval plus a governance-validator change, and must be applied by a human-run migration, not by an agent.

verdicts.reasoning:
WHAT I READ: all 126 files in database/supabase/migrations (000_baseline.sql + 073-197); 163_d2_live_data_leak_rls.sql in full; 164_d4_tenant_role_guc.sql in full; 107_security_rls_hardening_and_payment_uniqueness.sql:1-140; 078_password_set_intents.sql; 100_app_discovery_foundation.sql:110-160; 173_v1_gift_card_issuance_lifecycle.sql; scripts/validators/foundation-sql-policy-residue-validator.mjs; scripts/validators/rls-force-coverage-validator.mjs; tests/executable/tenant-redteam-postgres.test.mjs; services/api-gateway/src/routes/auth.ts:860-1050; apps/identity-platform/src/lib/auth/cookies.ts:110-135 and src/app/api/auth/set-password/route.ts:1-110; .github/workflows/production-deploy.yml; database/supabase/config.toml.

REPLAY METHOD: I wrote an ordered-event replay (CREATE POLICY / DROP POLICY / ALTER TABLE ENABLE|DISABLE|FORCE RLS / DROP TABLE, interleaved by byte offset within each file, files in filename order with 000_baseline first). Independent result: 680 final policies, 110 true-predicate, 19 without a TO clause. The claim's 680/110 match exactly; its "18" is 19.

REFUTATION AVENUE 1 — LATER-MIGRATION FIX: tested and failed to refute. No later DROP POLICY, CREATE OR REPLACE, ALTER, or REVOKE touches any of the 19. 163 rewrites 12 other tables; 164 only ADDS app_tenant permissive policies (permissive policies OR together, so they cannot restrict PUBLIC) and adds FORCE RLS (which affects only the table owner, not anon). I also checked for dynamic DDL that my regex replay could miss: the only `EXECUTE format(... POLICY ...)` sites are 102:341, 139:398, 143, 145, 151:273-275, 152:269, 153:226/252, 164:66 — none of them targets the 19 tables' policy names. There are zero `AS RESTRICTIVE` policies in the entire migration set, so nothing AND-restricts these permissives.

REFUTATION AVENUE 2 — UNREACHABLE CODE: failed to refute for the live tables. pages and collections are actively queried by the gateway (services/api-gateway/src/routes/pages.ts:310,379,694,723,780 and routes/resource-search.ts:102,155); audit_logs is actively written by middleware/rbac.ts:388, routes/admin.ts:128,167,330,354, routes/operations.ts:112, lib/internal-compliance.ts:137. auth_password_set_intents is live at routes/auth.ts:900,909,942. Partially succeeded for app_collections/app_collection_items/app_featured_placements/app_discovery_events (app-marketplace is a frozen non-deploy target per CLAUDE.md) and fully succeeded for gift_cards (dead legacy table, see corrected_claim).

REFUTATION AVENUE 3 — EARLIER GUARD: none exists for direct PostgREST access. This attack bypasses the gateway entirely, so verifySiteOwnership, the tenant-guarded Supabase client, and route-level RBAC are all irrelevant. There is no RESTRICTIVE policy and no CHECK constraint that blocks it.

REFUTATION AVENUE 5 — GRANT REALITY: this is the load-bearing precondition and I could not refute it. 000_baseline.sql contains ZERO GRANT/REVOKE statements (it is a --no-owner/--no-privileges pg_dump), so the ACL state is not in-repo. However the repository states its own grant posture in two places: (a) 107_security_rls_hardening_and_payment_uniqueness.sql:5-8 — "policies were named 'Service role ...' but OMITTED `TO service_role`, so they evaluated USING(true) for the anon and authenticated PostgREST roles → customer password hashes, session tokens, and password-reset tokens were readable with the public anon key"; (b) tests/executable/tenant-redteam-postgres.test.mjs:188 seeds `GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO anon, authenticated, service_role` as the modelled production posture. 163_d2_live_data_leak_rls.sql:202-216 adds explicit REVOKEs for exactly 11 tables + super_admin_allowlist, which only makes sense if anon/authenticated held those grants — and confirms the remaining 19 tables were never revoked. database/supabase/config.toml:[api] shows the Data API enabled over schema "public". So under the project's own threat model the grants are held.

WHY THE SEVERITY DROPS FROM S0: (1) the claim's money framing is refuted — gift_cards is inert. (2) 6 of the 19 (plans, employee_roles, employee_permissions, contact_submissions, leads, analytics_events) are deliberate, documented, allowlisted design, not defects; naming them inflates the count by a third. (3) The one genuinely S0-shaped table, auth_password_set_intents, is a chain that does not complete on the evidence: set-password/route.ts:46-70 trusts an unsigned `lb_password_set_intent` cookie whose only authority is the DB row, so a forged INSERT would set an arbitrary user's password and mint a session (:93) — but the table FKs to users_custom(id), and both users_custom (only policy: 107:34, TO service_role) and public.users (only policy: 000:27954, id = auth.uid()) are closed to PUBLIC, so the attacker has no demonstrated way to learn a victim's (users_custom.id, verified email) pair. sites.user_id is exposed via public_read_published_stores but FKs to public.users (000_baseline.sql:23075), not users_custom. (4) The anon key is NOT published by this codebase: no source file references NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY, no next.config.ts exposes it via an `env` block, and no Supabase browser client is constructed anywhere in apps/ — so despite production-deploy.yml:430-431 injecting it into all five Vercel builds, Next will not inline an unreferenced NEXT_PUBLIC_ var into a client bundle. Exploitation therefore requires separately obtaining the anon key.

WHY IT IS NOT REFUTED: the described condition unambiguously holds at replay-final. Cross-tenant read AND write of pages, collections, collection_products, onboarding_attempts and store_surveys, plus audit_logs INSERT forgery and ai_usage read/insert, are all live and reachable for any principal holding the anon key or any GoTrue-issued user JWT — exactly the threat model migrations 107 and 163 were written against. The governance gate cannot catch this: foundation-sql-policy-residue-validator.mjs:41-43 blanket-exempts every baseline true-policy as "legacy residue", and :45-54 classifies a policy as "service_role-only" purely by NAME (`service_role*`, `*_service_all`) without ever checking for a TO clause — the precise bug 163's own header describes.
