verdicts.corrected_claim: `POST /v1/storefront/:subdomain/orders` (defined at services/api-gateway/src/routes/storefront/checkout-payment-routes.ts:251, registered via services/api-gateway/src/routes/storefront/public-routes.ts:763, mounted at services/api-gateway/src/index.ts:752) is genuinely unauthenticated: `api.use('/*', authMiddleware)` is not registered until services/api-gateway/src/index.ts:779, and Hono composes handlers in registration order, so the storefront handler returns before auth (and before csrfProtection at :780 and protectedMutationIdempotency at :781) ever runs. It is publicly routed at api.letbuyy.com (services/api-gateway/wrangler.toml:220-224). It requires no customer session (`requireCustomerSession` is bound only to `/customer/*` at services/api-gateway/src/routes/storefront.ts:70-76), no Turnstile (`requireValidTurnstile` is wired only to registration/contact/review paths — services/api-gateway/src/routes/storefront/public-routes.ts:1322, customer-registration.ts:48, customer-engagement-routes.ts:712 and :1245), and no cart-bound signed handoff. The shipped storefront really does use it: apps/storefront-runtime/src/app/store/[subdomain]/checkout/page.tsx renders checkout-client.tsx, which POSTs to `/api/orders` at line 414, which proxies via apps/storefront-runtime/src/app/api/orders/route.ts:48 to `storefront.createOrder` = `POST /storefront/{subdomain}/orders` (packages/typescript/api-client/src/index.ts:5429-5430). A signed-handoff variant exists in parallel and is NOT used by the shipped UI: services/api-gateway/src/routes/checkout.ts (mounted index.ts:753, `checkoutSigningSecret` at :87, `invalidHandoff` at :104); migration 166's own header (database/supabase/migrations/166_d6_checkout_handoff_inventory.sql:3-4) records the hosted-checkout signing cutover as HUMAN-REQUIRED. Inventory IS hard-committed before payment, and — correcting the claim upward on this axis — for EVERY payment method, not just COD: the per-item loop at database/supabase/migrations/166_d6_checkout_handoff_inventory.sql:221 calls `commit_inventory_reservation` unconditionally, which does `SET available = GREATEST(available - qty, 0)` at database/supabase/migrations/141_executable_inventory_reservations.sql:212. COD additionally lands as `status = 'confirmed'` (166:199). This is replay-final: only 073, 000_baseline and 166 define `create_order_with_inventory_reservations`, 170 (`170_v1_shipping_rates_gst.sql:161`) only calls it, and no migration through 197 adds a trigger or constraint on `orders` that would require a checkout session. HOWEVER the claim's "un-bot-gated" framing omits two live throttles: a route-scoped per-IP limiter `authRateLimit` (20 POSTs / 5 min, keyed on CF-Connecting-IP) applied to exactly this path at services/api-gateway/src/routes/storefront/public-routes.ts:748-751 — registered before the handler at :763, so it does apply — and the global query-cost leaky bucket at services/api-gateway/src/index.ts:684-688 (cost 5 per POST, 20 pts/s, capacity 200), which does not skip this path (services/api-gateway/src/index.ts:356-371). Both fail closed in production (503 RATE_LIMIT_UNAVAILABLE) and their KV backend is configured (`RATE_LIMIT_KV_FALLBACK = "on"`, CACHE bound at wrangler.toml:313-316). Impact is unauthenticated inventory exhaustion / fake-order DoS with no money movement and no data exposure — an S1 availability-and-integrity defect and a real R-11/ART-14 violation, not an S0.
verdicts.reasoning: I read services/api-gateway/src/index.ts:620-800 and confirmed the mount ordering exactly as claimed (storefront at :752, authMiddleware at :779) — and in Hono a handler registered earlier that returns a Response terminates the chain, so authMiddleware, csrfProtection (:780) and protectedMutationIdempotency (:781) never execute for this path. I then tested every refutation avenue in order. (1) LATER-MIGRATION FIX: I enumerated every migration defining or touching the order-creation chain. `create_checkout_order` is defined in 073 and last redefined in 170_v1_shipping_rates_gst.sql:31; `create_order_with_inventory_reservations` is defined in 073, 000_baseline and last in 166_d6_checkout_handoff_inventory.sql:8 — 170 only CALLS it (170:161), and 173/174 reference it in comments only. I scanned all migrations 167-197 for triggers or constraints on `public.orders` and found none. So 166 is the replay-final body: status CASE at :199, unconditional `commit_inventory_reservation` at :221. (2) UNREACHABLE CODE: the route is mounted, the gateway has a production custom_domain route `api.letbuyy.com` (wrangler.toml:220-224), and I found no featureGate/killSwitch covering `/storefront/:subdomain/orders` — the only gates on that prefix are `appPlatformKillSwitch`/`extensionsFeatureGate` on `/storefront/:subdomain/checkout/extensions` (index.ts:722-723) and graphQL gates. (3) EARLIER GUARD — this is where the claim is materially incomplete. public-routes.ts:746-751 carries an explicit `// SECURITY: rate-limit checkout payment POSTs per-IP using authRateLimit (20/5min)` block registered on `/:subdomain/orders` BEFORE registerStorefrontCheckoutPaymentRoutes at :763, so it is in the chain. authRateLimit = 20 req / 300s (rateLimit.ts:1132-1136), keyed by CF-Connecting-IP (rateLimit.ts:954-956), which is edge-set and not spoofable. The global query-cost limiter also applies (index.ts:684-688) — I read shouldSkipGatewayQueryCostLimit (index.ts:356-371) and `/storefront/:subdomain/orders` is NOT in the skip list, only `/storefront/:subdomain/orders/contact` is. Additional real bounds I confirmed: the Zod schema caps items at 50 with quantity <= 999 (packages/checkout-core/src/index.ts:59-63); `assertOrderQuota` enforces a per-site monthly order ceiling when the plan defines `orders_monthly` (services/api-gateway/src/execution/order-execution.adapter.ts:154 and 374-391); `reserve_inventory` raises INSUFFICIENT_INVENTORY (141:128) so stock cannot go negative; and 166:131 raises `inventory level not found for product %` so only products with an inventory_levels row at an active location are orderable at all. Idempotency is not a mitigation — the claim key is caller-chosen and per-(site,key), so varying it yields a fresh order. (4) CONFIGURATION vs DEPLOYMENT: I verified the rate-limit backend is actually live rather than a config aspiration — no Upstash is provisioned, but `RATE_LIMIT_KV_FALLBACK = "on"` is set in [env.production.vars] and the CACHE KV namespace is bound at wrangler.toml:313-316, and checkRateLimitKeys (rateLimit.ts:840-864) uses the KV fallback in production. Had that binding been absent, the route would fail closed with 503 and the finding would have been REFUTED at runtime; it is not. (5) GRANT REALITY: not applicable — this is not a policy claim; the RPC is SECURITY DEFINER invoked by the gateway's service-role client (order-execution.adapter.ts:158). I also independently verified the shipped-UI assertion end to end rather than taking it on trust, and verified that the ART-14 signed-handoff implementation genuinely exists in parallel (routes/checkout.ts, verifyHandoff/CHECKOUT_SIGNING_SECRET) and is simply not on the storefront's submit path — storefront-runtime holds a cart_token (cart-context.tsx:43,153-154) but never presents it at order creation, and there is no redirect to CHECKOUT_ORIGIN anywhere in apps/storefront-runtime. Two corrections to the claim: it is UNDERSTATED on the pre-payment commit (that is not COD-specific — Razorpay orders also hard-decrement inventory at creation, before any payment), and OVERSTATED on both the guard inventory (a per-IP throttle exists and is enforced) and the severity class. S0 in this program denotes direct money loss, auth bypass to privileged data, or cross-tenant breach; this vector moves no funds, reads no data, and crosses no tenant boundary — it is a business-logic availability/integrity attack. Net severity S1.
verdicts.exploit_preconditions: Attacker needs only: (a) a published store subdomain — enumerable, and `loadPublishedStore` is the only tenant gate; (b) product UUIDs, which are free from the unauthenticated `GET /v1/storefront/{subdomain}/products` listing on the same router; (c) any syntactically valid customer name/email/phone/Indian address (Zod-shaped only, never verified) and a fresh >=8-char idempotencyKey per request; (d) target products must have an inventory_levels row at an active location, otherwise 166:131 aborts the whole order. No credential, cookie, cart token, CSRF token, or Turnstile solve is required, and CORS is irrelevant to a server-side caller. Throughput ceiling per source IP is 20 orders / 5 min (authRateLimit) with at most 50 line items x 999 units each, i.e. up to ~1,000 distinct SKUs zeroed per 5 minutes per IP; `reserve_inventory` caps each line at current on-hand, so the attacker reads stock from the public product listing and requests exactly that. The limiter is per-IP, so a distributed source removes the ceiling entirely. UNKNOWN without live DB/telemetry access: whether production stores actually populate inventory_levels rows (if most do not, orders 500 instead and the vector collapses to a functional-outage finding); the real distribution of `orders_monthly` entitlements, which sets the per-site order ceiling; and whether the CACHE-KV limiter's eventual consistency lets a single IP materially exceed 20/5min in practice.
verdicts.remediation: Minimal correct fix, in the order that closes the most exposure per unit of risk: (1) Require a server-side cart binding on the public order route — thread the existing `cart_token` the storefront already holds (apps/storefront-runtime/src/context/cart-context.tsx:153) into StorefrontCreateOrderSchema, and in checkout-payment-routes.ts:251 derive `items` from the server cart row rather than from `body.items`, rejecting any request whose token is absent, expired, or bound to a different site. This restores R-11/ART-14 intent without the DNS/signing cutover that migration 166 flags HUMAN-REQUIRED, and it is the only change that removes the arbitrary-item-list primitive. (2) Add `requireValidTurnstile(c, body)` at the top of that handler, mirroring the existing usage at public-routes.ts:1322 — this is the missing bot gate and is a low-risk, self-contained edit. (3) Tighten the throttle: the current authRateLimit (20/5min per IP) is a login-shaped limit reused for order creation; add a per-site and per-product-per-window ceiling so a distributed source cannot zero a catalogue, since a per-IP limit alone cannot bound this. (4) Separately, and requiring ARB sign-off because it changes canonical ledger behaviour: move the unconditional `commit_inventory_reservation` at 166:221 behind payment confirmation for non-COD methods, leaving reserve-with-TTL (the reservation sweeper already exists at services/queue-workers/src/inventory-reservations.ts) to hold stock until `confirm_order_payment_with_ledger` runs — R-11 explicitly requires reserve-with-TTL rather than pre-payment hard decrement. Authority classes: items 1-3 are ordinary application-code changes under the route-ownership rules; item 4 touches a SECURITY DEFINER money/inventory RPC and the checkout state machine and therefore needs ARB approval plus a paired rollback migration, per the canonical-ledger rules in AGENTS.md.

obligations.obligation: Commencement architecture - the DPDP Act 2023 and DPDP Rules 2025 are only PARTIALLY in force. G.S.R. 843(E) (13 Nov 2025) commenced ONLY s.1(2), s.2 (definitions), ss.18-26 (Data Protection Board), s.35, ss.38-43 and s.44(1)&(3). Sections 3-5, 6(1)-(8)&(10), 7-10, 11-17, 27 (except 27(1)(d)), 28-34, 36, 37 and 44(2) commence 18 months after Gazette publication; s.6(9) and s.27(1)(d) at 12 months. G.S.R. 846(E) mirrors this: Rule 1(2) - Rules 1, 2 and 17 to 21 in force on publication; Rule 1(3) - Rule 4 at one year; Rule 1(4) - Rules 3, 5 to 16, 22 and 23 at eighteen months.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: YES - but the substantive duties (notice, consent, security, breach, erasure, rights, SDF, transfer) are NOT YET enforceable against LetBuyy. Only the definitions and the Board's constitution are live; Rules 17-21 that are live are Board-internal (appointment, salaries, meetings, digital office, staff) and impose nothing on LetBuyy.
obligations.in_force_status: Partially in force. Substantive Chapter II/III duties NOT in force as of 2026-08-16; commence on/about 13-14 May 2027. Consent Manager provisions on/about 13-14 Nov 2026.
obligations.note: This is the single most important finding: build now, but there is no DPDP penalty exposure today. s.33 and the Schedule of penalties are themselves in the 18-month bucket, and ss.27(1)(a)-(c) and 28-34 are too, so the Board currently has no adjudicatory power over data-fiduciary breaches. Rules text: https://www.meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/11/53450e6e5dc0bfa85ebd78686cadad39.pdf

obligations.obligation: DECISIVE QUESTION - Data Fiduciary vs Data Processor. s.2(i): 'Data Fiduciary means any person who alone or in conjunction with other persons determines the purpose and means of processing of personal data.' s.2(k): 'Data Processor means any person who processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary.' The test is WHO DETERMINES PURPOSE AND MEANS - not who holds the database, not the contract label, not who custodies funds. Consequence: the Act imposes NO direct statutory duty on a Processor. Breach notice (s.8(6)/Rule 7), erasure (s.8(7)), rights response (ss.11-14), grievance redressal (s.8(10)) and DPO publication (Rule 9) are all duties OF THE DATA FIDUCIARY; s.8(7)(b) requires the Fiduciary to 'cause its Data Processor to erase'; s.8(2) requires a valid contract before engaging a processor; Rule 6(1)(f) requires safeguards flow-down in that contract.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: DEPENDS - and it splits by data set, not by company. (1) For a merchant's customer order/address/phone data used solely to run that merchant's store, LetBuyy is most likely a Data Processor and the merchant the Data Fiduciary. (2) LetBuyy is a Data Fiduciary IN ITS OWN RIGHT (or jointly - s.2(i) expressly says 'alone or in conjunction with other persons') for any processing whose purpose IT sets: cross-tenant analytics/benchmarking, cross-merchant fraud/risk scoring, ML training, its own product telemetry, its own marketing to shoppers, unilaterally-set retention schedules, or a single shopper identity shared across storefronts. (3) LetBuyy is unambiguously a Data Fiduciary for its own merchant-account holders' personal data.
obligations.in_force_status: s.2 definitions ARE in force now (from 14 Nov 2025). The consequences that flow from the classification (ss.8-17) are not in force until ~13-14 May 2027.
obligations.note: What it turns on, concretely: (a) does LetBuyy decide the PURPOSE for anything beyond executing merchant instructions; (b) does it decide the MEANS in more than a technical-implementation sense (retention periods, what is collected, who else sees it, secondary use); (c) does it use tenant data for its own account. s.8(1) makes a Data Fiduciary responsible 'irrespective of any agreement to the contrary' - merchants cannot push their responsibility onto LetBuyy, and LetBuyy cannot buy processor status by calling itself one in the MSA. There is NO GDPR Art.26-style joint-controller allocation mechanism. CAUTION: Illustration (I) to s.8(7) treats Y, operator of an online marketplace ('an e-commerce service provider'), as the Data Fiduciary for a customer who registered on it. This classification is precisely what decides who owes erasure and breach notice: a Processor's exposure is contractual/indemnity only, a Fiduciary's is statutory and penalty-bearing.

obligations.obligation: Notice (Rule 3): notice must be presented and understandable INDEPENDENTLY of any other information; in clear and plain language give at minimum (i) an itemised description of the personal data and (ii) the specified purpose(s) and specific description of the goods/services or uses enabled; and give the particular communication link for the website/app plus a description of other means to (i) withdraw consent 'with the ease of doing so being comparable to that with which such consent was given', (ii) exercise Act rights, (iii) make a complaint to the Board.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: DEPENDS - owed by whoever is the Data Fiduciary. If the merchant is the Fiduciary for shopper data, LetBuyy must SHIP the notice/consent UI as a product capability so merchants can comply; LetBuyy owes it directly for merchant-account signup.
obligations.in_force_status: NOT in force. Rule 3 (and s.5) commence ~13-14 May 2027.
obligations.note: 'Independently of any other information' means the consent notice cannot be buried in T&Cs or a cookie banner. Withdrawal parity is an explicit UX mandate.

obligations.obligation: Consent Manager (s.6(9), Rule 4, First Schedule): a Consent Manager must be a company INCORPORATED IN INDIA with net worth not less than Rs 2 crore, registered with the Board, independently certified as interoperable against Board-published standards, must ensure the shared data is 'not readable by it', must keep the consent record for at least 7 years, must not sub-contract or assign its obligations, acts in a fiduciary capacity toward the Data Principal, and must avoid conflicts of interest with Data Fiduciaries. Change of control requires prior Board approval.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: NO - unless LetBuyy chooses to become a registered Consent Manager. Using a Consent Manager is a channel available to Data Principals, not a mandatory intermediary for Data Fiduciaries. LetBuyy should NOT market any feature as a 'consent manager' without registration.
obligations.in_force_status: Rule 4 and s.6(9) commence ~13-14 Nov 2026 (12 months). Not in force now; registration cannot even be applied for until then.
obligations.note: The Board will publish the application particulars on its website once Rule 4 commences.

obligations.obligation: Data principal rights and response timelines. s.11 right to access (summary of personal data being processed + processing activities + the identities of ALL other Data Fiduciaries and Data Processors with whom the data has been shared, with a description of what was shared). s.12(1)-(2) right to correction, completion and updating. s.12(3) right to erasure - on request the Fiduciary 'shall erase her personal data unless retention of the same is necessary for the specified purpose or for compliance with any law for the time being in force'. s.13 right to grievance redressal (and the Data Principal must exhaust it before approaching the Board). s.14 right to nominate. Rule 14(1) requires publishing the means of making a request and the identifier required; Rule 14(3) prescribes a grievance-redressal response period 'not exceeding ninety days'.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: DEPENDS - owed by the Data Fiduciary. Either way LetBuyy must build request intake, identity resolution against Rule 14(5) 'identifier' (customer ID, email, mobile), and downstream erasure fan-out across tenant data, backups and sub-processors.
obligations.in_force_status: NOT in force. ss.11-14 and Rule 14 commence ~13-14 May 2027.
obligations.note: IMPORTANT DIVERGENCE: PIB states Data Fiduciaries must respond to access/correction/erasure requests 'within ninety days', but the Rule 14(3) text prescribes the 90-day cap for the GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL SYSTEM, not for rights requests; the Rules prescribe no separate clock for an s.11/s.12 request. Do not hard-code 90 days as the rights SLA without legal sign-off. Note s.11(1)(b) requires disclosing every sub-processor - a real engineering requirement for a multi-tenant SaaS.

obligations.obligation: Breach notification (s.8(6), Rule 7). To each affected Data Principal: 'without delay', concise/clear/plain, via her user account or a registered communication channel, containing (a) description incl. nature, extent and timing of occurrence, (b) the consequences relevant to her, (c) mitigation measures implemented and being implemented, (d) safety measures she may take, (e) business contact information of a person who can respond to her queries. To the Board: (a) WITHOUT DELAY, a description incl. nature, extent, timing, LOCATION of occurrence and likely impact; and (b) WITHIN SEVENTY-TWO HOURS of becoming aware (extendable only on a written request to the Board): updated and detailed description, broad facts of the events/circumstances/reasons, mitigation measures implemented or proposed, any findings on who caused the breach, remedial measures to prevent recurrence, and a report on the intimations given to affected Data Principals.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: DEPENDS - the duty is the Data Fiduciary's. A Processor-LetBuyy owes contractual notification to the merchant; a Fiduciary-LetBuyy owes the Board and shoppers directly. Note Rule 7 has NO de-minimis threshold and no risk-of-harm filter: every personal data breach triggers it.
obligations.in_force_status: NOT in force. s.8 and Rule 7 commence ~13-14 May 2027.
obligations.note: Two-stage clock: immediate first notice, full report at 72 hours. Contrast with the CERT-In 6-hour clock which IS already binding today - CERT-In, not DPDP, is the operative incident-reporting deadline in August 2026.

obligations.obligation: Reasonable security safeguards (s.8(5), Rule 6): a Data Fiduciary shall protect personal data in its possession or under its control, INCLUDING in respect of any processing undertaken on its behalf by a Data Processor, by at minimum (a) encryption, obfuscation, masking or virtual tokens mapped to the data; (b) access control on the computer resources used by the Fiduciary or the Processor; (c) visibility via logs, monitoring and review to detect unauthorised access and enable investigation/remediation; (d) continuity measures such as data backups; (e) RETAIN SUCH LOGS AND PERSONAL DATA FOR A PERIOD OF ONE YEAR unless another law requires otherwise; (f) appropriate provision in the Fiduciary-Processor contract for reasonable security safeguards; (g) appropriate technical and organisational measures.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: YES in substance - LetBuyy will have to meet these whether Fiduciary or Processor, because Rule 6(1) extends the duty to processing 'on its behalf by a Data Processor' and Rule 6(1)(f) mandates contractual flow-down. Merchants will require it in the DPA.
obligations.in_force_status: NOT in force (Rule 6 commences ~13-14 May 2027). However IT Act s.43A + the SPDI Rules 2011 impose an analogous 'reasonable security practices' duty that IS in force today.
obligations.note: Rule 6(1)(e) is a RETENTION FLOOR, not a ceiling - a one-year minimum for security logs AND the associated personal data. It conflicts with naive 'delete everything on request' engineering.

obligations.obligation: Retention and auto-erasure (s.8(7)-(8), Rule 8, Third Schedule). Rule 8(1) three-year auto-erasure applies ONLY to specified classes: a Data Fiduciary who is an e-commerce entity having NOT LESS THAN TWO CRORE registered users in India; an online gaming intermediary with not less than fifty lakh users; a social media intermediary with not less than two crore users - for all purposes except enabling account access and access to stored virtual tokens usable to get money/goods/services. Rule 8(2): at least 48 HOURS' advance notice to the Data Principal before erasure. Rule 8(3), applying to EVERY Data Fiduciary: retain personal data, associated traffic data and other logs of the processing for a MINIMUM OF ONE YEAR from the date of processing for Seventh Schedule purposes, then erase, unless further retention is required by law.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: DEPENDS. Rule 8(1)'s 3-year rule almost certainly does NOT apply - LetBuyy is far below two crore registered users, and the Third Schedule note excludes 'a seller offering her goods or services for sale on a marketplace e-commerce entity'. Rule 8(3)'s ONE-YEAR MINIMUM retention DOES apply to every Data Fiduciary.
obligations.in_force_status: NOT in force. Rule 8 commences ~13-14 May 2027.
obligations.note: Rule 8(3) Illustration Case 1 is directly on point: an e-book platform 'must retain the order details, personal data, and logs of the processing (such as order confirmation, payment, and delivery events) for at least one year from the date of the transaction, EVEN IF X DELETES HER ACCOUNT'. Case 2 extends this to the cloud Data Processor. This is a hard floor against immediate hard-delete on an erasure request.

obligations.obligation: Significant Data Fiduciary (s.10, Rule 13). The Central Government notifies an SDF on the basis of volume and sensitivity of data processed, risk to Data Principals' rights, potential impact on sovereignty and integrity, risk to electoral democracy, security of the State and public order. An SDF must appoint an India-based Data Protection Officer answerable to the board of directors and acting as the grievance point of contact; appoint an independent data auditor; undertake a Data Protection Impact Assessment AND an audit ONCE EVERY TWELVE MONTHS and cause the person carrying them out to furnish the Board a report of significant observations; observe due diligence that technical measures including algorithmic software used for hosting, display, uploading, modification, publishing, transmission, storage, updating or sharing of personal data are not likely to pose a risk to Data Principals' rights; and under Rule 13(4) ensure that personal data SPECIFIED BY THE CENTRAL GOVERNMENT (on the recommendation of a committee including MeitY officials) and the traffic data pertaining to its flow IS NOT TRANSFERRED OUTSIDE THE TERRITORY OF INDIA.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: NO today. SDF status arises only by Government notification of a named entity or class. No SDF notification has been located as of 2026-08-16, and Rule 13(4)'s localisation bites only once the Government specifies the data categories - which it has not.
obligations.in_force_status: NOT in force. s.10 and Rule 13 commence ~13-14 May 2027. No SDF notified; no Rule 13(4) categories specified; no committee publicly constituted.
obligations.note: There is NO turnover or user-count threshold for SDF in either the Act or the Rules - it is purely discretionary notification. Rule 13(4) is the only DPDP hook for hard data localisation and it is doubly contingent.

obligations.obligation: Children's data (s.9, Rule 10, Rule 12, Fourth Schedule). 'Child' = an individual who has not completed EIGHTEEN years (s.2(f)). Verifiable parental consent is required before processing any child's personal data, with due diligence that the self-identified parent is an identifiable adult by reference to (a) reliable identity and age details already held by the Data Fiduciary, or (b) identity/age details voluntarily provided by the individual or through a virtual token mapped to such details issued by an authorised entity, including via a Digital Locker service provider. s.9 also bars tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children. Rule 12 and the Fourth Schedule exemptions cover clinical/mental-health establishments, healthcare and allied healthcare professionals, educational institutions, creches/day-care and school transport - NOT commerce.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: DEPENDS. If storefronts can be used by under-18s (gaming merch, school supplies, toys, apparel), LetBuyy and its merchants face an 18-year age gate plus verifiable parental consent with no commerce carve-out. This is the harshest DPDP requirement for consumer commerce.
obligations.in_force_status: NOT in force. s.9 and Rules 10-12 commence ~13-14 May 2027.
obligations.note: No Fourth Schedule exemption exists for e-commerce. Product decisions needed on whether storefronts are declared 18+ only, and on whether behavioural retargeting pixels may run at all where a child may be the user.

obligations.obligation: Cross-border transfer (s.16, Rule 15). s.16(1): the Central Government MAY, by notification, RESTRICT transfer of personal data by a Data Fiduciary for processing to such country or territory outside India as may be notified - a blacklist model, not an adequacy/whitelist model. s.16(2) preserves any other Indian law providing a higher degree of protection or restriction. Rule 15: personal data may be transferred outside India subject to the restriction that the Data Fiduciary meets such requirements as the Central Government may, by general or special order, specify in respect of making such personal data available to any FOREIGN STATE, or to any person or entity under the control of or any agency of such a State.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: NO restriction applies today. No country has been notified under s.16(1) and no order has been issued under Rule 15. Under DPDP as drafted, transfer abroad is permitted by default.
obligations.in_force_status: NOT in force. s.16 and Rule 15 commence ~13-14 May 2027, and even then remain inert until a notification or order issues.
obligations.note: DPDP is markedly MORE permissive on transfers than GDPR. s.16(2) is the trapdoor: sectoral rules that are stricter (RBI payment data, CERT-In logs) survive and continue to bind.

obligations.obligation: Penalties (s.33 read with the Schedule): up to Rs 250 crore for breach of the s.8(5) obligation to take reasonable security safeguards; up to Rs 200 crore for failure to give the Board or affected Data Principals notice of a personal data breach under s.8(6); up to Rs 200 crore for breach of the s.9 children's obligations; up to Rs 150 crore for breach of Significant Data Fiduciary obligations under s.10; up to Rs 50 crore residual for breach of any other provision of the Act or rules; Rs 10,000 for a Data Principal's breach of s.15 duties. Appeals lie to the Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT); Rule 22 requires digital filing with a fee equal to that under the TRAI Act, payable via UPI.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: YES once in force, and only against whoever is the DATA FIDUCIARY - a Data Processor is not a penalty subject under the Schedule.
obligations.in_force_status: NOT in force. s.33 and the Schedule are in the 18-month bucket (~13-14 May 2027).
obligations.note: The largest single penalty head is the security-safeguards failure (Rs 250 crore), not the breach-notice failure - which argues for prioritising Rule 6 controls over notification workflow in the build order.

obligations.obligation: GAP FINDING - IT Act s.43A and the SPDI Rules 2011 REMAIN IN FORCE. DPDP s.44(2), which omits IT Act s.43A and s.87(2)(ob) (the rule-making power under which the SPDI Rules were made), is in the EIGHTEEN-MONTH bucket, not the immediate one. Only s.44(1) (Finance Act 2017 / Appellate Tribunal) and s.44(3) (substitution of RTI Act s.8(1)(j)) are in force now.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: YES. Today's binding personal-data law for LetBuyy is IT Act s.43A (compensation for negligent failure to implement reasonable security practices for sensitive personal data), the SPDI Rules 2011 (published privacy policy, consent for sensitive personal data or information, designated grievance officer with one-month redressal, restrictions on disclosure and transfer), and IT Act s.72A - NOT DPDP.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE NOW. Repealed on/about 13-14 May 2027 when s.44(2) commences.
obligations.note: Any privacy programme scoped for August 2026 must be an IT Act / SPDI Rules programme with a DPDP-readiness overlay, not a DPDP programme. Note SPDI 'sensitive personal data or information' expressly includes passwords and financial information such as payment instrument details.

obligations.obligation: DECISIVE QUESTION - what triggers PA authorisation. RBI (Regulation of Payment Aggregators) Directions, 2025 (RBI/DPSS/2025-26/141, CO.DPSS.POLC.No.S-633/02-14-008/2025-26, dated 15 Sept 2025), para 4.i defines a Payment Aggregator as an entity that 'facilitates aggregation of payments made by customers to merchants through one or more payment channels through the merchant's interface (physical / virtual) for purchase of goods, services or investment products, AND SUBSEQUENTLY SETTLES THE COLLECTED FUNDS TO SUCH MERCHANTS.' Para 3.a: 'These Directions shall apply to all bank and non-bank entities undertaking the business of Payment Aggregator (PA) as defined herein.' Para 5: non-bank entities must obtain RBI authorisation before commencing PA business.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: NO on the facts described - LetBuyy appears OUTSIDE the PA licensing perimeter. The definition is conjunctive and turns on COLLECTING AND SETTLING MERCHANT FUNDS. Where the merchant is merchant-of-record on the merchant's own authorised PA (Razorpay) account, funds move customer -> Razorpay escrow -> merchant, and LetBuyy never receives, holds, nets against or settles those funds, LetBuyy does not undertake 'the business of PA'.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE. Effective 15 September 2025; supersedes the 2020/2021 PA-PG guidelines and the 2023 cross-border PA directions.
obligations.note: Operating PA business without authorisation contravenes the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. The facts that would DRAG LetBuyy inside the perimeter: routing settlement through any LetBuyy-controlled bank account; holding merchant balances even transiently; deducting platform fees out of merchant collections BEFORE settlement; LetBuyy-directed split settlement; store credit or wallet balances redeemable for money; or LetBuyy becoming merchant-of-record. The 0% transaction fee is helpful evidence of the model but is not itself the legal test - fund custody is.

obligations.obligation: Payment Gateway carve-out and the marketplace bar. Para 4.j defines a Payment Gateway as 'an entity that provides technology infrastructure to route and facilitate processing of a payment transaction without any involvement in handling of funds.' Para 10.g provides that a PG 'shall not fall within the scope of this MD', though a PG is ENCOURAGED to adopt the baseline technology recommendations in Annexure 1. Para 10.b: 'A PA business shall not carry out marketplace business.' Para 4 defines Marketplace as 'an e-commerce entity which provides an information technology platform to facilitate transactions between buyer(s) and seller(s)'. Para 13.f: a PA shall ensure a marketplace it onboards does not accept payments for a seller not onboarded on the marketplace's platform.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: YES - this is the express carve-out LetBuyy relies on. A pure technology layer with no fund handling is outside the Directions. LetBuyy should nonetheless voluntarily adopt the Annexure 1 baseline security recommendations because acquirers and PAs will require them contractually.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE (15 September 2025).
obligations.note: 'Without ANY involvement in handling of funds' is absolute - there is no de-minimis. Note also that if LetBuyy ever positioned itself as a marketplace AND aggregated payments it would be structurally barred from holding a PA licence under para 10.b.

obligations.obligation: Escrow rules and settlement timelines (paras 16, 18, Table 1). A non-bank PA shall maintain the funds collected on behalf of its merchants in a SEPARATE ESCROW ACCOUNT with a Scheduled Commercial Bank in India, usable only for authorised PA business. Table 1 sets permitted credits (payer receipts, inter-PA settlement, refunds for failed/disputed transactions, pre-funding from own or merchant funds, promotional incentives) and permitted debits (payments to onboarded merchants, refunds to payers, payment to another PA, commission to the PA, and third-party payment on a merchant's specific direction only where that merchant has annual turnover above Rs 40 lakh or export turnover above Rs 5 lakh). Interest may be earned only on the 'core portion'. Para 18.b: 'The escrow account shall not be operated for Cash-on-Delivery transactions.' SETTLEMENT: the 2025 Directions REMOVED the fixed regulatory T+n schedule - Table 1 now reads 'Credit to merchant's a/c: As per the agreement between the PA and the merchant. Such an agreement should be fair, equitable and must transparently mention the settlement timelines.'
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: NO directly - escrow duties sit on the authorised PA (Razorpay). RELEVANT indirectly: LetBuyy's COD money path must never touch PA escrow rails, any platform-fee deduction from merchant proceeds is not a permitted escrow debit (only 'commission to PA' is), and there is no longer any regulatory T+n LetBuyy can assume.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE (15 September 2025). Existing non-bank PAs must migrate to the escrow arrangement within two months of authorisation. This is a change from the erstwhile 2020 guidelines which pegged settlement to date of shipment/delivery/refund.
obligations.note: Two engineering consequences: (1) the COD prohibition means LetBuyy's COD flow must be entirely outside the PA rails, consistent with merchant-collects-cash; (2) do NOT hard-code a T+n assumption in payout/reconciliation logic or merchant-facing copy - read it from the merchant's PA agreement. Note also that PSS Act s.23A settlement-finality protection attaches only AFTER authorisation.

obligations.obligation: Card-on-file / tokenisation mandate. RBI circular 'Restriction on Storage of Actual Card Data' (RBI/2022-2023/95, CO.DPSS.POLC.No.S-760/02-14-003/2022-23), issued under PSS Act ss.10(2) and 18: with effect from 1 October 2022, NO ENTITY IN THE CARD TRANSACTION OR PAYMENT CHAIN OTHER THAN THE CARD ISSUERS AND/OR CARD NETWORKS SHALL STORE CoF DATA, and any previously stored data had to be purged before that date. Limited exceptions: merchants or Payment Aggregators may retain CoF information for a maximum of T+4 days or until settlement, whichever is earlier, SOLELY for settlement of guest-checkout transactions; acquiring banks could retain until 31 January 2023. The PA Directions Annexure 1 s.2.1 adds that 'the customer card credentials shall not be stored within the database or the server accessed by the merchant', and para 10.e bars ATM PIN as an authentication factor for card-not-present transactions.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: YES. LetBuyy is an entity in the card transaction chain by virtue of hosting checkout. LetBuyy must never store PAN or any CoF data; saved-card functionality must be implemented exclusively via network tokens issued by the card networks and surfaced through Razorpay.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE since 1 October 2022.
obligations.note: Stricter than PCI DSS: PCI would permit encrypted PAN storage; RBI simply forbids it for non-issuers and non-networks. Verify separately whether last-four-digits plus card-issuer-name display remains permitted - that permission sits in the earlier tokenisation circulars and was not confirmed verbatim in this research.

obligations.obligation: Current version and the SAQ A vs SAQ A-EP determinant. PCI DSS v4.0.1 is the ONLY active version (v3.2.1 retired 31 Mar 2024; v4.0 published Mar 2022 and retired 31 Dec 2024; v4.0.1 published June 2024 as a limited revision adding no new or deleted requirements); all 51 future-dated v4.x requirements became effective 31 March 2025; an RFC on the next iteration ran 3 June - 20 July 2026 but no v4.1 or v5 has been published. SAQ A (v4.0.1 r1) covers card-not-present merchants who have COMPLETELY OUTSOURCED all account-data functions to PCI DSS compliant third parties and who do not store, process or transmit account data in electronic form on their systems or premises. BOTH a URL redirect and a TPSP-provided embedded payment page/iframe can qualify for SAQ A. The v4.0.1 script-security eligibility criterion - that the merchant has confirmed its site is not susceptible to attacks from scripts - applies ONLY to merchants whose webpage includes a TPSP's embedded payment page or form (e.g. an iframe), NOT to pure redirect merchants. Per FAQ 1588 that confirmation may be satisfied EITHER by using techniques such as those in Requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 OR by obtaining confirmation from the PCI DSS compliant TPSP that its solution, implemented per its instructions, includes techniques protecting the merchant's payment page from script attacks. Requirements 6.4.3, 11.6.1 and 12.3.1 were removed FROM SAQ A ONLY - they remain in the standard. ASV external scanning (Req 11.3.2) applies to SAQ A merchants in BOTH the redirect and iframe models. SAQ A-EP applies where the merchant's own website DOES affect the security of the transaction (direct post, JavaScript-created payment forms, or inability to confirm script safety) but the merchant does not store account data - a substantially broader requirement set including Requirement 1 network security controls.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: DEPENDS on the checkout LetBuyy ships. Redirect to Razorpay's hosted page => merchants stay SAQ A and the script criterion does not even engage. Embedded Razorpay iframe/SDK => merchants stay SAQ A ONLY if script-attack safety is confirmed, most easily via a Razorpay attestation. LetBuyy JS that creates, populates, intercepts or overlays the payment form, or arbitrary merchant/theme/app scripts injected onto the payment page => pushes merchants to SAQ A-EP.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE. v4.0.1 is the active version; SAQ A r1 supports requirements effective 1 April 2025.
obligations.note: CONCRETE PRODUCT CONSEQUENCE: LetBuyy's theme/app system permitting arbitrary third-party scripts on the checkout page is the single biggest risk of forcing every merchant from SAQ A to SAQ A-EP. Mitigations: strict CSP, script allow-listing, SRI, and no custom scripts on payment pages. A script provider is NOT a TPSP for SAQ A purposes if its only service is scripts unrelated to payment processing that cannot affect account-data security. Final SAQ eligibility is determined by the merchant's ACQUIRER, not by PCI SSC. PCI DSS is contractual, not statutory - but RBI PA Directions para 9 makes PCI-DSS compliance a regulatory condition for PAs, which flows down to LetBuyy contractually.

obligations.obligation: DECISIVE QUESTION - electronic commerce operator and s.52 TCS. CGST s.2(44): 'electronic commerce' means the supply of goods or services or both, including digital products, over digital or electronic network. s.2(45): 'electronic commerce operator' means any person who owns, operates or manages digital or electronic facility or platform for electronic commerce. s.52(1) is the operative charge: 'every electronic commerce operator, not being an agent, shall collect an amount calculated at such rate not exceeding one per cent... of the net value of taxable supplies made through it by other suppliers WHERE THE CONSIDERATION WITH RESPECT TO SUCH SUPPLIES IS TO BE COLLECTED BY THE SAID OPERATOR.' Current rate 0.5% CGST + 0.5% SGST (1% IGST for inter-State).
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: NO for TCS. The s.52(1) test is cumulative: (a) is an ECO, (b) not being an agent, (c) supplies made THROUGH it, AND (d) the consideration for those supplies IS TO BE COLLECTED BY THE OPERATOR. A SaaS platform that never collects consideration on behalf of sellers fails limb (d) and therefore has NO TCS liability, no s.24(x) compulsory registration as a tax collector, no GSTR-8 and no GSTR-9B. Whether LetBuyy is an 'ECO' at all under the broader s.2(45) is a SEPARATE and arguable question, since s.2(45) is not conditioned on collecting money - the counter-argument being that each merchant owns and operates its own storefront (own domain, own merchant-of-record status, own PA account) and LetBuyy supplies software rather than operating a platform for electronic commerce.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE. s.52 operative since 1 Oct 2018; rate reduced to 0.5%+0.5% from 10 July 2024. s.24(x) was narrowed to ECOs 'required to collect tax at source under section 52' by the CGST (Amendment) Act 2018, w.e.f. 1 February 2019.
obligations.note: Two adjacent traps: (1) s.9(5) makes the ECO liable to pay tax AS IF IT WERE THE SUPPLIER for NOTIFIED SERVICES ONLY (Notification 17/2017-CT(R) as amended: radio-taxi and passenger transport, hotel accommodation, housekeeping, restaurant service, and local delivery services w.e.f. 22 Sept 2025) - it does NOT apply to goods, so it does not reach a goods storefront. (2) s.24(ix) compulsory registration of suppliers selling through an ECO applies only where that ECO is required to collect TCS - so if LetBuyy collects no consideration, LetBuyy's merchants are not forced into registration on that ground (see also Notification 34/2023-CT exempting small goods suppliers through ECOs). No CBIC circular squarely addresses storefront SaaS providers.

obligations.obligation: E-invoicing (IRN and QR) under Rule 48(4) CGST Rules read with Notification 13/2020-CT as amended. The current threshold is aggregate annual turnover EXCEEDING Rs 5 CRORE in any financial year from 2017-18 onwards, mandatory with effect from 1 August 2023 (Notification 10/2023-CT dated 10 May 2023). E-invoicing applies to B2B supplies to registered persons, exports, deemed exports and SEZ supplies - it does NOT apply to B2C supplies. Exempt classes under Rule 48(4) include banks, insurers, financial institutions and NBFCs, goods transport agencies, passenger transport, admission to cinema exhibition, SEZ units and Government departments and local authorities.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: DEPENDS, and per-merchant not per-platform. The obligation attaches to each MERCHANT based on that merchant's own AATO. For a typical D2C storefront selling to unregistered consumers, e-invoicing is NOT triggered at all because those are B2C supplies. LetBuyy must (a) capture each merchant's e-invoicing applicability flag and (b) route only B2B, export and SEZ invoices to an IRP.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE. Rs 5 crore threshold since 1 August 2023. No 2026 notification lowering the threshold below Rs 5 crore was located on official sources.
obligations.note: This materially reduces LetBuyy's build scope: the IRN pipeline is a B2B feature for the minority of merchants above Rs 5 crore who also sell to registered buyers. Separately, Notification 14/2020-CT requires a DYNAMIC QR CODE on B2C invoices for suppliers with AATO above Rs 500 crore w.e.f. 1 December 2020 (see Circular 146/02/2021-GST) - far above LetBuyy's merchant base.

obligations.obligation: IRN reporting time limit: with effect from 1 April 2025, taxpayers with AATO of Rs 10 crore and above are not allowed to report e-invoices older than 30 DAYS from the document date on the IRP portals. The restriction covers Invoices, Credit Notes and Debit Notes; the IRP hard-blocks IRN generation beyond the window with an error.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: DEPENDS - applies per-merchant, only to merchants with AATO of Rs 10 crore or more who are also within the e-invoicing mandate. Merchants between Rs 5 crore and Rs 10 crore must generate IRNs but are not currently subject to the 30-day cut-off.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE since 1 April 2025 (the same restriction previously applied at Rs 100 crore from 1 November 2023).
obligations.note: Engineering consequence: back-dated invoice or credit-note generation must be blocked or alerted at 30 days for affected merchants, because a missed IRN can never be generated afterwards and the document is then not a valid invoice under Rule 48(5) - which in turn destroys the recipient's ITC.

obligations.obligation: Invoice retention and immutability. CGST s.36: every registered person required to keep and maintain books or records under s.35(1) shall retain them until the expiry of SEVENTY-TWO MONTHS FROM THE DUE DATE OF FURNISHING OF THE ANNUAL RETURN for the year pertaining to such accounts and records; a person party to an appeal, revision or other proceeding must retain for one year after final disposal, or for the 72-month period, whichever is LATER. Rule 56(16) extends preservation to all invoices, bills of supply, credit and debit notes and delivery challans, kept at every related place of business and accessible at every place where maintained digitally. A tax invoice cannot be edited once issued - corrections are effected only by credit or debit note under s.34 or by amendment in the GSTR-1 amendment tables.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: YES in substance. LetBuyy's immutable-invoice design is aligned with the statute. The effective retention floor is roughly six years nine months from the end of the financial year (FY end, plus annual return due date of 31 December, plus 72 months), extended by any litigation.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE.
obligations.note: This retention obligation is a lawful basis to refuse DPDP erasure of invoice-level personal data: both s.8(7) and s.12(3) carve out retention 'necessary for compliance with any law for the time being in force'. Design erasure as a redaction-plus-tombstone over the invoice record, not a delete.

obligations.obligation: Credit notes and amendments. CGST s.34(1): a credit note may be issued where the taxable value or tax charged in a tax invoice EXCEEDS the taxable value or tax payable, where goods are returned by the recipient, or where goods or services are found deficient. s.34(2): details of a credit note must be declared in the return for the month during which it was issued, but NOT LATER THAN THE THIRTIETH DAY OF NOVEMBER following the end of the financial year in which the supply was made, or the date of furnishing the relevant annual return, whichever is EARLIER. Proviso substituted with effect from 1 October 2025 by s.126 of the Finance (No. 7) Act 2025: no reduction in the supplier's output tax liability is permitted if (i) the input tax credit attributable to the credit note, where availed, has not been reversed by the recipient (registered recipient), or (ii) the incidence of tax on such supply has been passed on to any other person (all other cases).
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: YES in substance - refund and return flows must emit credit notes, must respect the 30 November cut-off for the year of supply, and must not silently reduce output tax where the new proviso conditions are unmet.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE. The 30 November date has applied since 1 October 2022 (Finance Act 2022 s.102, Notification 18/2022-CT). The output-tax-reduction proviso applies from 1 October 2025. A further s.34(1) discount clause inserted by s.154 of the Finance Act 2026 is NOT YET NOTIFIED.
obligations.note: For a B2C storefront the recipient is usually unregistered, so limb (ii) - tax incidence passed on - is the live constraint: a refund that actually returns the tax to the consumer supports the output-tax reduction; a partial refund or a store-credit refund may not.

obligations.obligation: Place of supply for goods and the CGST+SGST vs IGST split, plus HSN reporting. IGST s.10: where the supply involves movement of goods (by the supplier, the recipient or any other person), the place of supply is the LOCATION OF THE GOODS AT THE TIME AT WHICH THE MOVEMENT TERMINATES FOR DELIVERY TO THE RECIPIENT; on bill-to/ship-to, where goods are delivered on the direction of a third person, that person is deemed to have received the goods and the place of supply is that person's principal place of business; where there is no movement, it is the location of the goods at delivery; s.10(1)(ca) (inserted by the IGST (Amendment) Act 2023) addresses supplies to UNREGISTERED persons by reference to the address on record. IGST s.8 (intra-State, supplier location and place of supply in the same State/UT) => CGST+SGST; s.7 (inter-State) => IGST. HSN per Notification 78/2020-CT: minimum 4 digits where AATO is up to Rs 5 crore (mandatory for B2B), minimum 6 digits where AATO exceeds Rs 5 crore (both B2B and B2C), maximum 8 digits.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: YES in substance. LetBuyy's tax engine must derive the split from (merchant's registered State) versus (delivery State), not from billing address; must handle bill-to/ship-to; and must enforce per-merchant HSN digit minimums. GSTR-1/1A Table 12 Phase 3 requires HSN selection from a dropdown (no manual entry), splits the HSN summary into B2B and B2C from May 2025, and applies value validations against Tables 4A, 4B, 6B, 6C, 8, 9A, 9B, 9C, 15 and 15A.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE. Note also the 56th GST Council (3 September 2025) rate restructure to two main slabs of 5% and 18% plus a 40% demerit rate, effective 22 September 2025.
obligations.note: The 22 September 2025 restructure means any hard-coded 12% or 28% slab in LetBuyy's tax tables is stale; a 40% rate has also been added to the IRP tax-rate master. HSN advisory: https://tutorial.gst.gov.in/downloads/news/updated_advisory_hsn_table12_25042025.pdf

obligations.obligation: DLT registration stack under TCCCPR 2018 (6 of 2018) as amended by the Second Amendment Regulations 2025 (1 of 2025, No. RG-25/(25)/2023-QoS, 12 Feb 2025). Substituted Regulation 3: every Access Provider shall ensure any commercial communication using its network takes place ONLY using registered headers or number resources from the special series; and 'No Sender, who is not registered with any Access Provider for the purpose of sending commercial communications under these regulations, shall make any commercial communication' - breach permits suspension or disconnection of ALL the Sender's telecom resources. Amended 2(bw): any commercial communication by a Sender NOT REGISTERED with any Access Provider is deemed UCC per se. The stack is: Principal Entity (Sender) registration on DLT with an Access Provider, Header (sender ID, alphanumeric string of maximum eleven characters) registration, Content Template registration, Consent Template registration, and scrubbing against the Preference Register and Consent Register. Content template rules in the Schedule: variables capped at thirty characters unless justified, a MINIMUM THIRTY PER CENT of the content template must be fixed content, and one Content Template must not be linked with more than one Header; URLs, APKs, OTT links and call-back numbers are scrubbed against Sender-uploaded whitelists supported by an undertaking that they are not malicious. Chain traceability under Regulation 22: not more than two telemarketers (one with Aggregator Function, one with Delivery Function); misuse of headers or content templates triggers immediate suspension of the Sender's traffic across all Access Providers.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: DEPENDS on who the 'Sender' is. If LetBuyy sends SMS under its own header on behalf of merchants, LetBuyy is the Principal Entity/Sender and must be DLT-registered. If each merchant registers its own header, LetBuyy is at most a Registered Telemarketer/aggregator in the chain. Either way LetBuyy must model header, template ID, variable limits and the 30%-fixed-content rule as first-class data in its notification system.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE. TCCCPR 2018 in force; the Second Amendment came into force thirty days after Gazette publication except regulations 8, 17, 20(a)-(b) and 21(b), which came into force at sixty days. A DRAFT Third Amendment Regulations 2026 is out for consultation (draft consultation paper 13 March 2026) and is NOT in force.
obligations.note: TCCCPR applies to SMS and voice traversing Access Providers' networks. It does NOT currently regulate OTT messaging such as WhatsApp - that is governed by Meta's contract plus, from 2027, DPDP consent. Detailed operational procedures live in each Access Provider's Code of Practice under the co-regulatory model.

obligations.obligation: Promotional vs transactional vs service classification as amended in 2025. 2(bt) TRANSACTIONAL: a message or voice call to its Customer or Subscriber IN RESPONSE TO A CUSTOMER-INITIATED TRANSACTION WITHIN THIRTY MINUTES of the transaction - OTP from banks and non-bank entities like e-commerce, app logins, transaction alerts and confirmations, balance alerts post completion of a transaction, refund information; not promotional; no explicit consent required. 2(bh) SERVICE: (i) to its Customer or Subscriber providing information on a product or service, its warranty, product recall, software upgrade alerts, safety or security of the product used or purchased, periodic balance alerts, and INFORMATION REGARDING DELIVERY OF GOODS OR SERVICES - not promotional, no explicit consent; or (ii) to a Recipient to facilitate or complete a commercial transaction involving ongoing purchase or use, AFTER obtaining Explicit Consent, which 'shall be for seven days or as directed by the Authority'. A transactional message containing service information is treated as a Service Message. 2(au) PROMOTIONAL: contains promotional material or advertisement; the Sender MUST give an opt-out mechanism IN THE SAME MESSAGE; and 'if promotional content is mixed with any type of Transactional or Service Message, such Message shall be treated as a Promotional Message'. Promotional messages are delivered only to subscribers who have not blocked the applicable category in the Preference Register or who have given consent in the Consent Register; explicit digital consent overrides registered preferences. New proviso to 2(ah): inferred consent 'shall not extend beyond duration / discharge of the contract between the Sender and the Recipient', and for commercial messages may be clearly and reasonably inferred from the registered Content Template.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: YES in substance. Concrete mapping: OTP and order-placed confirmation within thirty minutes = Transactional. Shipment dispatched, out for delivery, delivered, return approved = SERVICE message under limb (i), NOT transactional, because they fall outside the thirty-minute window. Abandoned-cart nudges, discount codes, festival offers, and ANY order update carrying a coupon = Promotional, requiring preference scrubbing, consent, and an in-message opt-out.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE (thirty or sixty days after Gazette publication of the 12 February 2025 amendment).
obligations.note: HIGH-RISK PRODUCT PATTERN: appending a promo code or a 'shop again' CTA to a delivery-confirmation SMS reclassifies the ENTIRE message as Promotional, which then requires consent and preference scrubbing plus an opt-out in the same message, and risks header/template suspension. Keep transactional and service templates strictly clean of marketing content.

obligations.obligation: WhatsApp Business Platform requirements (contractual, not statutory). Opt-in: 'You may only contact people on WhatsApp if: (a) they have given you their mobile phone number; and (b) you have received opt-in permission from the recipient confirming that they wish to receive subsequent messages or calls from you.' When collecting opt-in a business must clearly state that the person is opting in to receive communication from the business, clearly state THE BUSINESS'S NAME, and comply with applicable law; the business determines the method (SMS, website, IVR, in-person or paper). Meta recommends per-message-category opt-in and requires clear instructions for opting out of specific categories. All requests to block, discontinue or opt out, whether made on or off WhatsApp, must be honoured including removing the person from contact lists; Meta may reactively evaluate a business's opt-in flows including user feedback. Business-initiated conversations may only be started using an APPROVED MESSAGE TEMPLATE; free-form replies are permitted only within the 24-hour customer service window, and automated experiences must provide prompt, clear, direct escalation to a human. Templates must be categorised MARKETING, UTILITY or AUTHENTICATION; mixed content (an order update carrying a promotion, or a feedback survey with promotional content) is MARKETING. Only authentication templates may deliver one-time passcodes and must use Template Library templates with a copy-code or one-tap OTP button, no URLs, media or emojis, and parameters capped at fifteen characters. Since 1 July 2024 Meta recurrently re-categorises approved templates; from 16 April 2025 businesses warned for categorisation abuse no longer receive 24-hour notice.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: YES if LetBuyy ships WhatsApp notifications. LetBuyy must persist per-shopper, per-category opt-in with provenance (source, timestamp, the business name shown at capture), enforce the 24-hour window, honour opt-outs across channels, and keep utility templates entirely free of promotional content.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE as Meta contract terms (policy updated November 2024 per Meta's documentation). Not Indian law; does not displace TCCCPR (which does not currently reach OTT) or, from 2027, DPDP consent.
obligations.note: Prohibited categories include illegal products or services, firearms, drugs, endangered species, body parts, multi-level marketing, payday loans and debt collection, discriminatory messaging and sexually explicit content; regulated verticals (alcohol, tobacco, over-the-counter drugs, online and real-money gambling) are permitted only in limited countries, must not target users under 18, and require local licensing. Breach risk is commercial (number ban, WABA suspension), not regulatory.

obligations.obligation: DECISIVE QUESTION - is there a general Indian data-residency mandate? NO. There is no current Indian law requiring commerce data or personal data generally to be stored in India. DPDP s.16 is a blacklist mechanism (the Central Government MAY restrict transfers to notified countries) with NO country notified, and it is not in force until ~May 2027. DPDP Rule 15 permits transfer subject to requirements the Government may specify about making the data available to a foreign State or its agencies - no such general or special order has issued, and Rule 15 is not in force. DPDP Rule 13(4) imposes a no-transfer-outside-India restriction ONLY on SIGNIFICANT DATA FIDUCIARIES and ONLY for personal data and associated traffic data categories the Central Government specifies on a committee's recommendation - no SDF has been notified, no categories specified, and Rule 13 is not in force.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: NO general mandate applies. A single ap-south region is therefore an ARCHITECTURAL AND CONTRACTUAL CHOICE for LetBuyy's commerce and personal data today, not a legal requirement - subject to the two specific exceptions below.
obligations.in_force_status: No general mandate in force as of 2026-08-16. DPDP transfer provisions commence ~13-14 May 2027 and remain inert until a notification or order issues.
obligations.note: Note DPDP s.16(2): any other Indian law imposing a HIGHER restriction on transfer survives - which is exactly how the RBI and CERT-In mandates below continue to bite. The residency answer is therefore 'no for commerce data, yes for logs and payment data'.

obligations.obligation: EXCEPTION 1 - RBI payment data localisation (specific and in force). Circular 'Storage of Payment System Data', RBI/2017-18/153, DPSS.CO.OD No.2785/06.08.005/2017-2018, dated 6 April 2018: all authorised payment system providers shall ensure that THE ENTIRE DATA RELATING TO PAYMENT SYSTEMS OPERATED BY THEM IS STORED IN A SYSTEM ONLY IN INDIA. Per the RBI FAQ the scope reaches banks as payment system operators or participants plus 'system participants, service providers, intermediaries, payment gateways, third party vendors' engaged by authorised entities; 'entire data' covers end-to-end transaction details, customer information (name, contact details, identity numbers), payment-sensitive data (customer and beneficiary account details), credentials such as OTPs and passwords, and transaction metadata such as timestamps and amounts. Processing abroad is permitted but the resulting data shall be stored only in India after processing, and must be DELETED FROM THE SYSTEMS ABROAD AND BROUGHT BACK TO INDIA not later than one business day or 24 hours from payment processing, whichever is earlier. For cross-border transactions a copy of the domestic component may also be stored abroad if required. The PSO bears responsibility for compliance by the intermediaries and vendors it engages. The PA Directions 2025 expressly require PAs to comply with this circular.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: DEPENDS - not directly (LetBuyy is not an authorised PSO), but DERIVATIVELY and contractually: if LetBuyy sits in Razorpay's payment chain as a technology vendor or gateway, Razorpay is obliged to ensure LetBuyy's compliance for any payment system data LetBuyy touches or stores.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE since 2018 and actively enforced - RBI has imposed and subsequently lifted supervisory business restrictions citing this circular.
obligations.note: This is SPECIFIC to payment system data - it does not reach product catalogues, storefront content, themes or CMS assets. The hard boundary question for LetBuyy is an ORDER RECORD carrying both commerce fields and payment references/customer identifiers: legal review is needed on whether such a record is 'data relating to payment systems'. Practically, keeping order and payment tables in ap-south removes the question. Circular text: https://rbi.org.in/scripts/NotificationUser.aspx?Id=11244

obligations.obligation: EXCEPTION 2 - CERT-In Directions, 28 April 2022 (No. 20(3)/2022-CERT-In, under IT Act s.70B(6)), binding on 'service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporate and Government organisations'. Direction (i): connect to the NTP server of NIC or NPL (or traceable sources that do not deviate) to synchronise all ICT system clocks. Direction (ii): 'shall mandatorily report cyber incidents as mentioned in Annexure I to CERT-In WITHIN 6 HOURS of noticing such incidents or being brought to notice about such incidents.' Direction (iii): designate a Point of Contact to interface with CERT-In in the Annexure II format, keep it updated, and comply with CERT-In orders including near-real-time information requests. Direction (iv): 'shall mandatorily enable logs of all their ICT systems and maintain them securely FOR A ROLLING PERIOD OF 180 DAYS and the same SHALL BE MAINTAINED WITHIN THE INDIAN JURISDICTION', to be provided to CERT-In with any incident report or on direction. Direction (v): data centres, Virtual Private Server providers, cloud service providers and VPN service providers must register and retain accurate subscriber/customer information for five years (or longer if mandated) after cancellation or withdrawal of registration.
obligations.applies_to_letbuyy: YES, DIRECTLY AND TODAY. LetBuyy is both a 'body corporate' and a 'service provider'. This - not DPDP - is the binding incident-reporting clock (6 hours) and the binding log-residency mandate (180 days within Indian jurisdiction) in August 2026.
obligations.in_force_status: IN FORCE since 28 June 2022 (60 days after issue), and from 25 September 2022 for MSMEs and for the subscriber-validation mechanism.
obligations.note: THIS IS THE ANSWER TO 'is ap-south a legal requirement': for ICT LOGS, yes - they must be maintained within Indian jurisdiction for a rolling 180 days, so shipping logs to a non-Indian observability SaaS is a live compliance issue. The 6-hour CERT-In clock is far tighter than DPDP's future 72-hour Board report, so incident runbooks must be built to 6 hours now. The PA Directions additionally require annual cyber-security audit by a CERT-In empanelled auditor and monthly incident reporting for PAs, which flows down contractually to LetBuyy.

india.summary: The single most consequential finding is that the DPDP Act 2023 is still overwhelmingly NOT in force as of 2026-08-16. MeitY's commencement notification G.S.R. 843(E) of 13 November 2025 brought into force only section 1(2), section 2 (definitions), sections 18-26 (the Data Protection Board), sections 35, 38-43 and section 44(1) and (3); every substantive obligation LetBuyy would engineer for - notice (s.5), consent (s.6), the general obligations of a Data Fiduciary including security and breach notification (s.8), children's data (s.9), Significant Data Fiduciary duties (s.10), data-principal rights (ss.11-14), transfer outside India (s.16) and the penalty regime (ss.28-34) - sits in the eighteen-month bucket and commences on or about 13-14 May 2027, with the Consent Manager provisions (s.6(9), Rule 4) at twelve months, on or about 13-14 November 2026. The DPDP Rules 2025 (G.S.R. 846(E)) mirror this exactly: only Rules 1, 2 and 17-21 are live, and those are Board-internal. Because DPDP s.44(2) is itself in the eighteen-month bucket, IT Act section 43A and the SPDI Rules 2011 have NOT been repealed and remain the operative personal-data security and grievance law binding LetBuyy today, alongside IT Act s.72A. What genuinely binds LetBuyy right now is therefore not DPDP but the CERT-In Directions of 28 April 2022 - a mandatory 6-hour cyber-incident report to CERT-In, NIC/NPL time synchronisation, a designated Point of Contact, and ICT logs enabled and maintained securely for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction. On the platform-versus-processor question, the statutory test is purely who "determines the purpose and means of processing" (s.2(i)) versus who processes "on behalf of a Data Fiduciary" (s.2(k)); it turns on decision rights, not on data custody, contract labels or fund flows, and s.2(i)'s "alone or in conjunction with other persons" means LetBuyy can be a joint Data Fiduciary while the merchant is one too - with s.8(1) making each responsible "irrespective of any agreement to the contrary" and no GDPR-style allocation mechanism available. In practice LetBuyy is likely a Processor for merchant-instructed order and customer data but a Data Fiduciary in its own right for its merchant account holders and for any cross-tenant analytics, cross-merchant fraud scoring, ML training, its own marketing or unilaterally-set retention - and that classification is what decides who owes erasure and breach notice, because the Act imposes no direct duty on a Processor at all. On payments, the RBI (Regulation of Payment Aggregators) Directions 2025 of 15 September 2025 define a PA by the conjunctive act of aggregating customer payments and "subsequently settl[ing] the collected funds to such merchants", and expressly carve out at paras 4.j and 10.g the payment gateway that "provides technology infrastructure to route and facilitate processing of a payment transaction without any involvement in handling of funds" - so a platform where the merchant is merchant-of-record on the merchant's own Razorpay account and LetBuyy never custodies funds sits outside the authorisation perimeter, with risk arising only if LetBuyy ever routes, holds, nets fees from, or splits merchant collections. The Directions also removed the fixed regulatory T+n settlement schedule, which is now purely contractual between PA and merchant. Two RBI rules reach LetBuyy indirectly: the card-on-file restriction (no entity in the card chain other than issuers and networks may store CoF data, since 1 October 2022) and the 2018 payment-data localisation circular, whose FAQ extends the "stored only in India" obligation through PSOs to their service providers, intermediaries, payment gateways and third-party vendors. On GST, the decisive TCS test in s.52(1) is cumulative and fails on its last limb for LetBuyy: TCS bites only "where the consideration with respect to such supplies is to be collected by the said operator", so a SaaS platform that never collects consideration owes no TCS, needs no s.24(x) registration, and files no GSTR-8 or GSTR-9B - though whether it is an "electronic commerce operator" at all under the broader s.2(45) remains arguable and unlitigated for storefront SaaS, and s.9(5) reaches only notified services, never goods. E-invoicing is far narrower than commonly assumed: the Rule 48(4) threshold remains AATO above Rs 5 crore since 1 August 2023, it applies only to B2B, export, deemed-export and SEZ supplies and never to B2C, so most D2C storefront sales sit outside it entirely, while the 30-day IRN reporting cut-off applies only at AATO of Rs 10 crore and above from 1 April 2025, and records must be retained 72 months from the annual-return due date under s.36. For PCI DSS, v4.0.1 is the only active version with all future-dated requirements effective since 31 March 2025, and both redirect and TPSP-iframe checkouts can keep merchants on SAQ A - the script-safety eligibility criterion applies only to the iframe case and can be discharged by a Razorpay attestation - but LetBuyy's theme and app system permitting arbitrary scripts on the checkout page is the concrete risk that would push every merchant to SAQ A-EP. For messaging, TCCCPR 2018 as amended on 12 February 2025 now confines "transactional" to messages within thirty minutes of a customer-initiated transaction, treats shipping and delivery updates as "service" messages, and reclassifies any transactional or service message carrying promotional content as wholly promotional - so appending a coupon to a delivery SMS is a direct compliance failure - while unregistered senders are deemed to be sending UCC per se. Finally on residency: there is no general Indian mandate requiring commerce or personal data to be stored in India, DPDP's transfer provisions are a not-yet-commenced blacklist mechanism with no country notified, and Rule 13(4)'s localisation applies only to Significant Data Fiduciaries for categories the Government has not yet specified, so a single ap-south region is an architectural and contractual choice for commerce data - but it IS a legal requirement for ICT logs under CERT-In and for payment system data under the RBI 2018 circular flowing down through Razorpay. Every legal conclusion in this brief is source material only and is marked LEGAL-REVIEW-REQUIRED.

RIGHTS-REQUEST RESPONSE SLA under DPDP. Rule 14(3) prescribes a period 'not exceeding ninety days' for the GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL SYSTEM; the PIB release glosses this as a 90-day deadline for access/correction/erasure requests. The Rules contain no separate clock for s.11 or s.12 requests. SETTLED BY: MeitY clarification or Data Protection Board guidance on the s.13(2) prescribed period; the Rule 14(3) text as gazetted is the primary source and it does not say what PIB says.

CONTROLLER/PROCESSOR ALLOCATION FOR MULTI-TENANT SaaS. No Indian regulator, court or Data Protection Board has issued guidance on whether a commerce SaaS provider is a Data Fiduciary, a Data Processor or a joint Data Fiduciary for a merchant's customers' data. SETTLED BY: MeitY guidance under the DPDP framework, or the first Board order once ss.27-34 commence. No such document exists as of 2026-08-16.

WHETHER A STOREFRONT SaaS IS AN 'ELECTRONIC COMMERCE OPERATOR' UNDER CGST s.2(45) at all, independent of the s.52 'collects the consideration' test. No CBIC circular addresses SaaS platforms where each merchant operates its own storefront and is merchant-of-record. SETTLED BY: a CBIC circular under s.168(1) or an advance ruling. The CBIC e-commerce FAQ at cbic.gov.in/resources/htdocs-cbec/gst/faq-e-commerce.pdf returned HTTP 500 and could not be retrieved in this pass.
